title: Component Forge
subtitle: Your own components, and the argument trap

intro.headline: A component is a function that returns a tree
intro.body:
There is no component class, no registration step, and no `props` object. You write an ordinary JavaScript function, its parameters are ordinary parameters with ordinary defaults, and whatever it `return`s becomes UI.

That simplicity moves the difficulty somewhere unexpected: to the **call site**. Because arguments can be passed by position *or* by name, one call can be structurally perfect and semantically wrong — and the validator will not say a word.

`Button("Save", "primary")` is that call. This world is about writing components, and about never being fooled by that line again.
intro.codeCaption: declare it, then call it two different ways
objectives: Declare a component with real JS parameters and defaults
End every component with an explicit `return`
Choose one of the three call forms and stay inside it
Extend a built-in component instead of replacing it

stages.title: Declare and return
stages.goal: A component is a function whose return value is a tree.

teach.text:
`function Name(params) { return Tree }`. That is the entire declaration syntax. No decorator, no `defineComponent`, no export.

The rule that catches everyone is the last word of it: **always end with an explicit `return`**. A body that builds a `Badge(...)` and then falls off the end really did build the node — and then discarded it. Nothing throws, nothing warns, the page is just missing a piece.

The mirror-image mistake is returning the name instead of a call. `return Badge` hands back the function itself; the renderer has no instruction to invoke it, so again: nothing.

code.caption: declaration, parameters, return — nothing else is required

infographic.title: What the last statement decides
rows: nothing — the node is built, then dropped
nothing — a bare name is a value, not a call

tips: Case is a readability convention only. `function chip(...)` renders exactly the same as `function Chip(...)`.

tips.text: A component with no `return` renders nothing and reports nothing. Check for it first whenever a component vanishes.

challenge.title: Four Chips, four outcomes
challenge.prompt: All four of these declare something called `Chip`. Exactly one puts a pill on the screen; the other three are silent no-ops, and no two of them fail the same way. Match each declaration to what it actually does.

right.label: A pill on the page — the node is built and then escapes the body
The node really is built, then dropped when the body ends
The component itself is handed back, and the renderer never calls it
A plain object — there is no registry to declare a component to

hints: Two of the four really do build a Badge node. Only one of those hands it back.
A component is a function. What must a function do for a value to escape its body?
Pair the one that works first, then separate the other three by *why* they fail: no `return`, a name instead of a call, or not a function at all.
stages.explain: A component is not a special kind of object — it is a plain function whose return value happens to be a tree. That is exactly why the missing `return` is invisible: the body ran, `Badge(...)` really did produce a node, and then the function ended and threw it away. Nothing is wrong enough to report. `return Badge` fails for the mirror reason: a bare name is the function itself, and the renderer never calls what it is handed. And the object-literal form has no meaning at all here — with no component registry, an object named `Chip` is just an object.

afterCode.caption: the shape to remember

codex.def: `function Name(p) { return Tree }` — a plain JS function that returns a component tree. No `return` means no output and no error.

stages.title: The signature is the API
stages.goal: Props are real JS parameters with real JS defaults — there is no props object.

teach.text:
Because a call site is an ordinary function call, the parameters are ordinary parameters. Give them JavaScript defaults with `=`, destructure them if you like, and read them by name inside the body.

There is nothing to reach into: `props.tone` cannot work because nothing ever builds a `props`. Read the parameter list and you know every prop the component takes and which one is positional.

State declared inside the body belongs to the *instance*, not the program. `$n = 0` in a component body is a declaration: the initializer runs once when that instance mounts, and every later re-render keeps whatever the user, an action, or an effect has written since.

code.caption: plain params, JS defaults, destructuring — all standard

code2.caption: two call sites, two independent $n atoms

infographic.title: Reading a signature
infographic.code: function Chip(label, tone = "neutral") { return Badge(label, { tone }) }

parts.text: Case is convention. What makes it a component is that it returns a tree.
Real JS parameters. There is no props object to reach into.
A plain JS default, used whenever the caller omits that argument.
Leave this off and the component renders nothing, silently.

tips: Destructured parameters work: `function Panel({ title, tone = "info" })` is a valid signature.

tips.text: `$n = 0` inside a body is a declaration, not an assignment that runs on every render. Two call sites get two independent atoms.

challenge.title: Declare it, then call it
challenge.prompt: Three slots: give `tone` a default, let the tree out, and call the component you just declared. Four of the chips are habits from other frameworks — leave them in the bank.

hints: Parameters are ordinary JavaScript. How do you give an ordinary JS parameter a default?
There is no props object — `label` and `tone` are already in scope inside the body.
The last slot sits in call position. It needs the name declared at the top of the file.
stages.explain: There is no props object because there is no framework layer standing between the call and the function — `Chip("Shipped", "success")` is just a call, so `label` and `tone` are just parameters and `= "neutral"` is just a JavaScript default. `default:` and `props.` are shapes from Vue and React that have nothing to bind to here. The payoff is that a component's signature is its complete, readable API: no separate prop declaration can drift out of sync with it.

codex.def: Component props are real JS parameters with real JS defaults (`tone = "neutral"`). There is no props object; destructured parameters work too.

preview.caption: the third pill never passed a tone — it took the default

stages.title: One call, one form
stages.goal: Pick one of the three argument forms per call, and know what position binds.

teach.text:
Every call picks exactly one of three forms:

- **canonical** — `Component(positional, { prop: value })`
- **all-positional** — `Component(a, b, c)`, binding in signature order
- **all-named** — `Component({ prop: value })`

All-positional is the sharp one. An unnamed argument binds to the *next prop in the signature*, whatever that happens to be. `Badge(label, tone, icon, size)` puts tone second, so `Badge("Live", "success")` is correct. `Button(label, onClick, variant, type, size, …)` puts **onClick** second — so `Button("Save", "primary")` hands the string to the click handler, renders the default style, and validates cleanly.

Never split one object between the two roles. Some components take a *leading* props object because their children are the trailing positional — `Grid({ columns: 12 }, [CardA(), CardB()])` — but that is still one form, not a mix of two.

code.src:
Button("Save", { variant: "primary" })      // canonical
StatCard("Revenue", "$48k", "up")           // all-positional
Button({ label: "Save", variant: "primary" }) // all-named
code.caption: three forms, three calls — never two forms in one call

columns.title: Slot two is onClick
columns.note: Signature: label, onClick, variant. "primary" becomes the handler — default styling, dead click, clean validator.

columns.title: Named, so order stops mattering
columns.note: One positional, every other prop named in the trailing object.

tips: All-positional is safe only when the props you want are adjacent and leading — `StatCard("Revenue", "$48k", "up")` is fine.

tips.text: Never split one object between the two roles. One call, one form.

challenge.title: Which calls do what they say?
challenge.prompt: Every one of these passes the validator. Switch ON only the calls where each argument actually lands on the prop the author meant.
challenge.help: Read the signature in your head before you flip anything. Leave the misrouted calls off.

switches.label: Button("Save", { variant: "primary" })
switches.detail: canonical: one positional, every other prop in the trailing object

switches.label: Button({ label: "Save", variant: "primary" })
switches.detail: all-named: one object, every prop by name

switches.label: Grid({ columns: 3 }, [Card([Text("A")]), Card([Text("B")])])
switches.detail: leading props object, children as the trailing positional

hints: For each call, say the signature out loud and ask what prop slot two is.
`Button(label, onClick, variant, …)` versus `Badge(label, tone, …)`. Only one of those makes a second positional string safe.
`StatCard(label, value, trend, …)` — a two-argument call never reaches `trend`.
stages.explain: Position is meaningful, so an unnamed argument binds to whatever prop comes next in the declaration order — nothing about the string `"primary"` marks it as a variant. `Badge("Live", "success")` and `Button("Save", "primary")` are structurally identical calls; only the two signatures differ, and that difference is the whole bug. `StatCard("Revenue", "up")` fails the same way one slot earlier: the tile renders with the value "up" and no trend. The canonical form exists precisely to make a call immune to its signature's order — name the prop and position stops mattering.

codex.def: `C(positional, { props })`, `C(a, b, c)` in signature order, or `C({ props })`. Pick one per call; never split an object between the two roles.

preview.program:
$app(Column([
  PageHeader("Same label, two argument forms", { breadcrumbs: false }),
  Card([
    SectionHeader("Button(\"Save\", \"primary\")", { subtitle: "all-positional: slot two is onClick" }),
    Button("Save", "primary"),
    Text("Plain button. The variant never arrived.", { tone: "muted", variant: "small" })
  ]),
  Card([
    SectionHeader("Button(\"Save\", { variant: \"primary\" })", { subtitle: "canonical: one positional, one trailing object" }),
    Button("Save", { variant: "primary" }),
    Text("Solid brand button, exactly as written.", { tone: "muted", variant: "small" })
  ])
]))
preview.caption: live — two buttons, one difference, no error message

stages.title: The Forge
stages.goal: Route every argument token into the role that actually binds it.

teach.text:
A call site is being forged: `Button(  __  , {  __  })`. Argument tokens are falling into it.

**Tap a lane to route the lowest token.** A token that carries its own name (`variant: "primary"`) belongs in the options object. The label `"Save"` belongs in the positional slot.

The bare `"primary"` belongs in neither. Send it to the positional lane and you will watch it wire itself to `onClick`. Let it fall instead — it only becomes a variant once you give it its name back.
tips: Anything with a colon in it is a named prop.

tips.text: Three misroutes ends the run. Letting a token fall costs nothing.

challenge.title: Route the tokens
challenge.prompt: Named tokens go in the options object. The label goes in the positional slot. The bare `"primary"` goes nowhere — let it fall.
challenge.note: Tap a lane at the bottom to route the lowest falling token.
challenge.winNote: Press Check to bank the XP.

fallback.prompt: `Button("Save", "primary")` renders a plain default button. Where did `"primary"` actually go?

options.label: Into the second positional slot — which the signature declares as `onClick`.
Into `variant`, but `"primary"` is not a valid variant value.
options.detail: `"primary"` is a perfectly valid variant. It simply never reached that prop.

options.label: Nowhere — arguments past the first are ignored unless they are named.
options.detail: Nothing is ignored. Every positional argument binds to the next prop in the signature.

options.label: Into `type`, the third prop in the signature.
options.detail: Off by one — the order is label, onClick, variant, type.

hints: A colon means the token names its own destination.
The bare `"primary"` has no home in this call. Do nothing and it falls away for free.
Tap the lane, not the token — the lowest token is the one that gets routed.
stages.explain: Routing is the whole model. A token that carries a name can sit anywhere inside the options object, because the name — not the position — decides what it binds to. A token with no name is bound by position alone, so it lands wherever the signature says the next slot is. That is why `"primary"` on its own has nowhere to go in a `Button` call: as a positional it becomes the click handler, and inside an object it is not a key/value pair at all. Giving it back its name is the entire fix.

codex.def: An unnamed argument binds to the next prop in the component's signature — so `Button("Save", "primary")` sets onClick, not variant.

stages.title: The prop that wasn't
stages.goal: Spot a named prop that quietly became a positional argument.

teach.text:
When you call **your own** component with a trailing object, the runtime has to decide what that object is: a bag of named props, or just a value you happen to be passing.

Its rule is mechanical. If any key in the object matches a parameter name, it is treated as named props. If **no** key matches, the whole object is forwarded as a positional argument instead.

That rule is what makes an opaque data payload or a slots bag work at all. The price is that a misspelled prop name is not an error — it is a differently shaped argument, arriving in the next positional slot. Built-in components validate their prop names, so a typo there is caught; your own components have no prop list to check against.

code.caption: one wrong letter, no diagnostic

infographic.title: How the trailing object is classified

steps.label: not a props bag
steps.note: so it is a value, not named props

tips.text: This flip applies to *your* components. Built-ins reject unknown prop names outright — `Badge("Live", { tint: "success" })` is a validation error.

tips: The runtime's strict mode logs a warning when it forwards an unmatched object. The default mode stays silent.

challenge.title: It renders. It is still wrong.
challenge.prompt: Every pill appears, nothing throws, the validator is clean — and one badge has lost its colour. Tap the token responsible.

hints: The program renders and nothing throws. So look for a name that matches nothing.
Check every key of an options object against the parameter list directly above it.
stages.explain: The runtime cannot tell a props bag from a payload by shape alone, so it uses the only signal available: do the keys name parameters? `tint` names neither `label` nor `tone`, so the object is classified as a value and slides into the second positional slot — `tone` becomes `{ tint: "success" }`, and `Badge` receives an object where a tone string belongs. The other three spans are all legal on purpose: `Chip("Refunded", "danger")` is an all-positional call, `Chip("Paid")` takes the default, and `Badge` inside the body is just the library component. This is the cost of the rule that lets you pass an opaque slots object at all — and it is why a prop typo on your own components is worth reading for twice.

codex.def: If a trailing object's keys match none of a custom component's parameters, it is forwarded as a positional argument instead of raising an error.

stages.title: Extend, don't replace
stages.goal: Wrap a built-in component by reusing its own name.

teach.text:
Declaring a component with a built-in's name is normally rejected — a program containing two different `Badge`s is unreadable. There is exactly one exception, and it is the useful one.

**If the body calls that same name, the declaration is a wrapper.** Inside its own body, the name resolves to the *built-in*, so the outermost call is yours and the innermost is the library's. It extends instead of recursing, and it terminates at depth one.

Write a `Badge` that pins every pill to the success tone, then render two of them. Same call sites everywhere else in the program — new behaviour.

code.caption: the inner Badge is the library's, not this one

layers.label: Badge("Shipped")
layers.note: call site — resolves to your declaration

layers.label: Badge(label, { tone: "success" })
layers.note: inside the body, the name is the built-in

tips: A `function` declared inside another component's body is scoped to it — component-local helpers never leak to the rest of the program.

tips.text: The exception is narrow. Reuse a built-in's name *only* when your body calls that same name; any other shadowing is a validator error.

challenge.title: Wrap the built-in
challenge.prompt: Extend the library `Badge` so every badge in this program renders with `tone: "success"`, then use it twice inside one `$app(...)`, stacked in a `Column`.

mustWhy: Declare the wrapper with the built-in's own name: `function Badge(label)`.
The body has to call `Badge(...)` — that inner call is what makes it a wrapper instead of an error.
Pin the tone in the trailing object: `{ tone: "success" }`.
Stack the two badges in a `Column([ ... ])`.

hints: You are allowed to reuse the name `Badge` — on exactly one condition.
Inside the body of `function Badge(...)`, the name `Badge` means the library one.
`function Badge(label) { return Badge(label, { tone: "success" }) }`, then call it twice inside `$app(Column([...]))`.
stages.explain: The validator's rule is a readability rule, not a technical limit: a shadowing declaration is rejected unless its body calls the shadowed name, because that pattern is unmistakably a wrapper rather than a replacement. The runtime cooperates by resolving the name to the built-in while it is evaluating the declaration's own body, which is what stops the wrapper recursing to the depth limit. A renamed wrapper — `SuccessBadge` — works equally well and is often clearer; the reason to keep the name is that every existing call site inherits the new behaviour with no edits.

afterCode.caption: outermost call yours, innermost call the library's

codex.def: A custom component may reuse a built-in's name only if its body calls that name — inside its own body the name resolves to the built-in, so it extends rather than recurses.

preview.caption: live — three call sites, none of them passing a tone

outro.headline: The call site stopped being a guess
outro.body: A component is a function that returns a tree, its parameters are its API, and every call picks one form and stays in it. `Button("Save", "primary")` will not fool you twice — and neither will a trailing object whose keys match nothing.
outro.nextHint: Next: data — turning a URL into a reactive bag your components can read while it loads.

badge.name: Forgemaster
badge.tagline: Routed every argument to the slot it meant.
